You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis

Details:
The test "closeEvents" is designed to check that two very close events generated by a switching function are both detected during an ODE integration step. The function g(t, y) returns (t - r1)*(r2 - t), with events expected at t = 90.0 and t = 135.0. The test first evaluates a step from a time before the first event (r1 - 0.5 * gap) to a time within the first event interval, then it checks for the detection of the first event and accepts the step ending exactly at that event time. Then it evaluates a subsequent larger step from there past the second event and asserts that the second event is detected.

The current bug report states that when two events occur very close to each other and the integration step crosses both events, the last event may be ignored, depending on the bracketing interval side chosen. This fits well with the test scenario, where two events are close (gap = 45) and the step spans chosen in the test might trigger this edge condition.

Inspecting the EventState.evaluateStep method, the step is subdivided into n substeps for checking events. The method looks for sign changes in the event function g(t, y) between ta and tb, solving for the root iteratively. In the presence of closely spaced events, the logic has a corner case handling between lines 191-197 to handle events "near ta" and "another event between ta and tb". It notes that the sign at ta can be wrong due to convergence thresholds and tries to compensate.

The critical part is that during the iteration, if a sign change is detected, a Brent solver tries to find the root of the switching function between ta and tb. If the found root is very close to the previous event time and also close to ta, the root is ignored (lines 219-223). This might suppress detection of the second event if it is very close to the first event time (within convergence tolerance).

After a root is found, pendingEventTime and pendingEvent are updated, and evaluateStep returns true indicating an event is pending but doesn't directly handle the detection of successive events tightly spaced.

In the stepAccepted method, when an event step is accepted, the state is updated at the event time, and the sign g0Positive is set to the direction "just after the event." This sets the basis for detecting the next event.

The issue likely occurs because the logic that suppresses roots very close to the previousEventTime (within convergence) may erroneously suppress detection of the second event when it occurs near in time to the first event, especially if the bracketing interval and step subdivision result in the event detection being shifted to the "wrong side" as stated in the comment lines 191-197. This aligns with the report's observation about the side of the bracketing interval affecting detection.

Hence, the bug arises due to the sign change detection and root finding logic ignoring or suppressing very closely spaced events detected within the convergence tolerance bounds, causing the last event in a pair of close events to be missed.

This explains why the test fails when the integration step spans from before the first to after the second event, and the second event is not properly detected.

No relevant clues or fixes appear in the unrelated recent bug reports. The failure is localized to the event detection logic in EventState.evaluateStep and the handling of pendingEventTime versus previousEventTime.

The test's scenario and bug report description strongly agree: close events with spacing less than or near convergence cause the second event to be ignored due to root finding and sign checks in evaluateStep. 

This is the root cause of the failure in EventState during ODE integration when two events occur close to each other.

Suggested locations for fixes will target the evaluateStep method and possibly stepAccepted to better handle closely spaced events.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
